rows.verified: Work equipment must be suitable for its intended use.
Equipment must be maintained in a safe condition and inspected where necessary.
Only people with adequate information, instruction and training should use work equipment.
Access to dangerous machinery parts should be prevented or movement stopped before a person reaches the danger zone.
Safeguards can include fixed or interlocked guards, emergency stops and isolation from energy sources.
Machines should be checked for defects and for the presence and condition of safeguards before use.
Maintenance and blockage-clearing should be planned so people are not exposed to moving or energised machinery.
Training and competence requirements must reflect the equipment, task and risks involved.
Safeguarding must match the actual machine, access needs, failure modes and residual risks; generic guarding is not sufficient.
Machinery-safety evidence is equipment- and task-specific and is not an exact parcel-level probability.
Employers must protect workers from health risks associated with display screen equipment use.
The DSE regulations apply to workers who use display screen equipment daily for continuous periods of an hour or more.
Employers must carry out a workstation assessment for workers who are DSE users.
Risks identified by the assessment should be reduced so far as reasonably practicable.
Work should be planned so intensive screen use is interrupted by breaks or changes of activity.
Employers must provide an eye and eyesight test for a DSE user who requests one.
Special glasses must be provided where an eye test shows they are needed only for the DSE viewing distance.
DSE users must receive training and information about posture, workstation adjustment, glare, breaks and reporting problems.
Assessment and equipment needs depend on the individual, workstation, work pattern and whether work is at home, in an office or hybrid.
DSE evidence is workstation- and user-specific and is not an exact parcel-level probability.
